The SHO should expect a caseload concentrated in **Faisalabad (19 cases)**, **Lahore (18 cases)**, and **Rawalpindi (10 cases)**, with smaller numbers in other districts [Document 1]. The case mix has shifted significantly: in 2026, **51 FIRs** involve a broad range of statutes, including the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), Arms Ordinance 1965, CNSA 1997, PECA 2016, and Punjab Domestic Violence Act—unlike 2024, when only 13 FIRs focused on PPC and Arms Ordinance [Document 2]. Arrests are rare, with **11 arrests recorded across 73 FIRs**, meaning 62 cases have no arrest [Document 3]. Crime reporting has slowed dramatically, with a **mean delay of 23.4 hours** in 2026 compared to **15 minutes** in 2024 [Document 4]. Weapon licensing is a critical issue: **30 of 32 recovered weapons** have no licence recorded, and 2 entries lack licence status entirely [Document 5].  

Accused individuals are mostly **unaged (75 of 92 have no age recorded)**, but those with ages range from **24 to 49 years** (mean 31.5) [Document 6]. Relationships between accused and complainants are sparse but notable: **15 of 24 entries** list the accused as a **stranger**, the most common relationship [Document 7]. In court, **32 of 33 cases** remain in progress, with only **1 case** reaching a verdict [Document 8].  

Priorities should include addressing **weapon licensing non-compliance**, investigating **delays in reporting crimes**, and improving **arrest rates** given the low current figure.
